The title does not provide supplementary information such as the analysis method, included study designs, update status, or living-review status. No evidence in the title indicates study designs or analysis details.

elements.quote: However, studies assessing their effectiveness in delivering primary prevention interventions for non-communicable disease prevention and control in LMIC settings are limited,[10], though this has been proven for developed countries.[11]
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the current state of knowledge and uncertainty by stating that studies assessing CHW effectiveness for NCD prevention in LMICs are limited, contrasting this with evidence from developed countries.

elements.quote: Considering this deficiency in availability of effectiveness parameters, a systematic review on effectiveness of CHW delivered primary prevention interventions for NCDs in developing countries was conducted by the authors.
elements.reason: The authors explicitly state the importance and need for conducting the review because of the deficiency of effectiveness data in LMIC settings and therefore conducted the systematic review.

elements.quote: Only four systematic reviews assessing this effectiveness in LMIC/ developing countries could be identified after review of published literature.[11-14]
elements.reason: The manuscript identifies existing systematic reviews (four) and thereby situates the current review in relation to prior reviews, explaining the landscape of prior evidence.

elements.quote: A community health worker (CHW) delivers NCD preventive services using informational as well as behavioural approaches. Community education and interpersonal communication on lifestyle modifications is imparted with focus on primordial prevention of NCDs and screening is conducted as part of early diagnosis and management.
elements.reason: The manuscript briefly describes how the intervention (CHW-delivered services) is intended to work—through informational and behavioural approaches, education, lifestyle modification counseling, and screening—constituting a proposed mechanism of action.
No evidence was found in the provided text that a logic model was presented or considered to show hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes.

elements.quote: Considering this deficiency in availability of effectiveness parameters, a systematic review on effectiveness of CHW delivered primary prevention interventions for NCDs in developing countries was conducted by the authors. This was conducted following the hypothesis that for NCD control programs employing a community health worker is more likely to be successful than routine care. This manuscript details the methodologies followed and reports on findings from this systematic review.
elements.reason: The authors state that they conducted a systematic review on the effectiveness of CHW-delivered primary prevention interventions for NCDs and state a hypothesis comparing CHW programs to routine care, which indicates the review objective. However, there is no explicit, structured statement of specific review question(s) using a question-formulation framework (e.g., PICO or explicit primary/secondary objectives), so the requirement is only partially met.

elements.quote: Interventions included community health worker led health education/health promotion (life style modification advice) for diabetes, cancer, cardiovascular diseases and stroke prevention. Health topics that were studied include healthy diet, physical activity/ regular exercise, tobacco consumption/ promotion of smoking cessation, alcohol consumption, management of type 2 diabetes/ hypertension, awareness for common cancers. Studies were excluded if the intervention was not adequately described to determine that it was a CHW intervention or if the effects were not properly described to determine whether the CHWs presence produced the effects.
elements.reason: The review specifies the population and interventions of interest (CHW-led health education/promotion for various NCDs and risk factors) and exclusion criteria, and Table 1 provides examples of populations, interventions and controls. However, the authors do not present an explicit PICO-formatted planned comparison statement (e.g., 'Population X compared to Y with intervention Z vs comparator A') nor a clear, complete PICO table; thus planned comparisons are described in the text but not explicitly framed using PICO, making this only partially satisfied.

elements.quote: Only randomised controlled trials (community based randomised controlled trial, cluster randomised trials) published in the last 15 years (2000-2015) were included in the review. ... Trials about CHWs working in NCD related promotional, preventive or curative primary healthcare in LMICs/ developing countries were included. ... A seven point inclusion criterion was followed to shortlist the articles. A research was considered eligible for inclusion if it followed a randomised controlled study design in community settings of low middle income countries with community health worker as intervention delivery person for general or high risk population for primary prevention of NCDs as compared to routine care or enhanced routine care as comparator.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies key study characteristics used for eligibility: study designs (randomised controlled trials, cluster RCTs), settings (community settings in LMICs/developing countries), intervention delivery (CHW), target populations (general or high-risk for primary prevention of NCDs), and the time window (2000-2015).

elements.quote: Only randomised controlled trials (community based randomised controlled trial, cluster randomised trials) published in the last 15 years (2000-2015) were included in the review. ... Searches of published literature ... were done ... without restriction to language: PubMed (2000-2015); Excerpta Medica Database (EMBASE) (2000-2015); OVID (2000-2015) and World PLOS Health Organization (WHO) library and Cochrane library. Clinical trials registers such as ClinicalTrials.gov ... were another source of information that were reviewed for relevant literature. ... Unpublished reports identified in a database or referenced in a publication in the initial search were also read.
elements.reason: The review states eligibility restrictions by dissemination year (2000-2015), explicitly states no language restriction, and that unpublished reports and trial registers were considered, addressing publication/report status criteria.

elements.quote: We recorded all missing secondary outcome data in the data extraction form and in the risk of bias table. One trial lacking baseline information collection by investigators was excluded from the meta-analysis.
elements.reason: The review documents that missing outcome data were recorded and that a trial lacking baseline information was excluded from meta-analysis, but it does not explicitly distinguish exclusions due to outcomes not being measured versus outcomes measured but not reported.

elements.quote: Meta-analyses were carried out separately for each outcome and type of study design (RCT/ cRCT). ... Meta-analysis was conducted only for interventions for which there were a minimum of two studies displaying sufficient homogeneity (I 2 statistic < 75%). ... The outcome abstraction from the trials was not limited to the primary outcome on which the trial was based. Efforts were made to pool results for all other reported outcomes ... Studies were pooled only if the outcomes had been measured in the same way by all studies.
elements.reason: The review specifies how studies were grouped for syntheses (by outcome and study design RCT/cRCT), pooling rules (same measurement, minimum two studies, I2 threshold), linking groupings to the comparisons and objectives.

elements.quote: Only randomised controlled trials (community based randomised controlled trial, cluster randomised trials) published in the last 15 years (2000-2015) were included in the review. The time period was limited to base evidence on recently conducted studies in light of recent shift in delivery of primary health care services towards NCDs in most of the developing countries. It is worthwhile to highlight that till 2000, focus of the primary care services of most of the governments has been on maternal and child health services, family planning services, tuberculosis and HIV/AIDS.
elements.reason: The review provides a rationale for the notable restriction on publication years (2000-2015), explaining the choice based on shifts in health service focus and relevance of recent evidence.

elements.quote: Full search strategy has been provided as supplementary material (S1 Text).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states that the full search strategy is available as supplementary material (S1 Text), indicating the complete strategies used are reported (though in supplement).

elements.quote: Only randomised controlled trials (community based randomised controlled trial, cluster randomised trials) published in the last 15 years (2000-2015) were included in the review. ... The time period was limited to base evidence on recently conducted studies in light of recent shift in delivery of primary health care services towards NCDs in most of the developing countries.
elements.reason: The authors report a date limit (2000-2015) and provide a justification linked to changes in primary health care focus, satisfying reporting of search limits and justification per eligibility criteria.
No citation of published search approaches or filters nor description of adaptations is provided in the available text.
No mention of natural-language processing or text-analysis tools to identify or refine search terms is found in the supplied evidence.
No tools for translating search strings between sources are specified in the provided text.
There is no description of any validation of the search strategy or validation studies in the retrieved evidence.
No peer review of the search strategy (e.g., PRESS) or description of such a process is reported in the available text.
Although a multi-stage search strategy is mentioned, there is no description that the search structure was not based on PICO nor is the final conceptual structure or its development described.

elements.quote: Two researchers (GJ, RP) under the supervision of one supervisor (JST) independently screened the titles and abstracts identified by the electronic searches for relevancy.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly reports the number of reviewers (two) who screened titles/abstracts and names the supervising third reviewer, addressing number of reviewers at screening stages.

elements.quote: Two researchers (GJ, RP) under the supervision of one supervisor (JST) independently screened the titles and abstracts identified by the electronic searches for relevancy.
elements.reason: The text explicitly states that the two reviewers performed title/abstract screening independently, indicating independence at that screening stage.

elements.quote: Disagreements during both stages were resolved by discussion or with intervention of the third reviewer (JST) who made the final decision.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the process used to resolve screening disagreements (discussion and third-reviewer adjudication).

elements.quote: Authors or trial investigators for further information were contacted for queries pertaining to methodology, study outcome, availability of trial reports (if results not yet published as journal article).
elements.reason: The text states that study investigators were contacted to obtain or confirm eligibility/methodological information.
No information is provided about methods used to translate abstracts or full articles for eligibility assessment.

elements.quote: The results of the searches were entered onto the reference management software, Endnote. [21] Multiple publications of the same study identified were grouped together and represented by a single reference. Titles and abstracts of all articles identified through the electronic searches were imported into EndNote and duplicates removed.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes use of EndNote for managing search results and removing duplicates, but does not describe use of automation tools for screening (e.g., machine-assisted screening), so description of automation integration is partial.
No information is given about externally derived classifiers, their versions/references, roles, or records removed before screening.
No information is given about any internally derived classifiers, their training, validation, or use.
No information is provided about use of machine-learning prioritisation tools or screening stopping/prioritisation rules.
No information is provided about use of crowdsourcing platforms in study selection.
No information is provided about use of previously screened datasets to eliminate records or how such datasets were derived.

elements.quote: As per methodology requirements, one reviewer abstracted data (GJ) and other reviewers confirmed accuracy (JST, SP, MS).
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly states how many reviewers were involved in data abstraction (one primary extractor plus three others who confirmed accuracy).

elements.quote: As per methodology requirements, one reviewer abstracted data (GJ) and other reviewers confirmed accuracy (JST, SP, MS). Reviewers independently dualrated study quality and applicability using established criteria.
elements.reason: The text indicates a single primary extractor with others confirming accuracy and states that reviewers independently rated study quality; however it does not clearly state that multiple data collectors independently extracted data from each report (independent dual data extraction for extraction itself is not explicitly reported).

elements.quote: Discrepancies were resolved through a consensus process wherein all four reviewers jointly analysed and discussed each article.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes the process used to resolve disagreements—consensus discussion among all four reviewers.

elements.quote: Where the change per group was not available [26, 30], we used end-values where randomisation was successful.[26] ... for which we contacted the study's primary author via email. We recorded all missing secondary outcome data in the data extraction form and in the risk of bias table.
elements.reason: The text reports that authors were contacted by email to obtain missing data and that missing data were recorded in extraction forms, describing the process for obtaining/confirming data from study investigators.
No information is provided about any automation tools used for data collection, their use, training, or validation.
The manuscript provides no details on methods used to translate articles for data collection.
No software or methods for extracting data from figures are specified in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: For interventions with multiple comparison groups, all groups that met the inclusion criteria were included in the review and meta-analyses.[31] ... because comparison groups we combined the relevant experimental and control groups to generate a single pair wise comparison.[31] ... Where the change per group was not available [26, 30], we used end-values where randomisation was successful.[26]
elements.reason: The manuscript describes decision rules for handling multiple comparison groups (including all eligible groups and combining groups to create single pairwise comparisons) and selecting end-values when change scores were unavailable.

elements.quote: Primarily it captured the trial's methodological approach as well as specifics regarding how effects of the intervention were assessed. Additionally, it also collected data on methodology used for CHW selection, training, terms used to describe the CHWandtheir supervision.
elements.reason: The authors describe several types of variables that were collected (methodological approach, effects assessment, CHW selection, training, terminology, supervision) and present a characteristics table (Table 1), but they do not provide a complete, itemized list with formal definitions of all other variables sought. Thus reporting is partial rather than fully listing and defining every variable.

elements.quote: For trials which had not accounted for clustering, sample size estimates were adjusted for design effect using an 'approximation method'.[27] Effective sample size was calculated for the comparison groups by dividing the original sample size by the design effect. Design effect was calculated as 1 + (M - 1) ICC, where M is the average cluster size and ICC is the intra-cluster correlation coefficient. If primary data was not provided, we attempted to find an appropriate ICC from the literature and adjusted the sample size accordingly.[28]
elements.reason: The manuscript describes explicit assumptions and procedures used when study information was missing/unclear (e.g. adjusting sample size for clustering using an approximation method and using ICCs from the literature).

elements.quote: Primary reviewer (GJ) developed detailed electronic data extraction tool in MS Excel. The tool was adapted from The Cochrane Public Health Group: Data Extraction and Assessment Template to collect information on all aspects deemed necessary as per MECIR standards[23] from studies included in the review.
elements.reason: The authors cite and describe adapting a specific data-extraction tool (The Cochrane Public Health Group: Data Extraction and Assessment Template) as the basis for determining which data items to collect.

elements.quote: Binary outcomes were reported as relative risk (RR) of outcomes in the intervention group compared to the control group. For continuous outcomes, and where baseline data were available, mean difference (MD) between the change in the intervention and control groups were reported. 95% confidence intervals (CIs) have been reported alongside all effect estimates.
elements.reason: The methods section explicitly states the effect measures used: RR for binary outcomes and MD for continuous outcomes, and that 95% CIs accompany estimates; Table 3/4 also labels outcomes with RR or MD.

elements.quote: The current study selected proportion of participants who became moderately active (MET minutes 600 minutes as lower benchmark) as a measure for physical activity. Jafar et al took 840 MET minutes as the lower benchmark for physical activity.
elements.reason: The review reports numerical thresholds used to interpret one outcome (physical activity MET-minute cut-offs). However, there is no explicit rationale provided for these thresholds or general thresholds/ranges used to interpret effect sizes across outcomes.
No text in the provided evidence describes methods used to re-express synthesized results using another effect measure (e.g., converting OR to RR or standardized mean difference to MD).
While the review states which effect measures were used (RR, MD), it does not provide a justification for the choice of these effect measures in the supplied evidence.

elements.quote: Studies were pooled only if the outcomes had been measured in the same way by all studies. Where the change per group was not available [26, 30], we used end-values where randomisation was successful.[26] 95% confidence intervals (CIs) have been reported alongside all effect estimates. Meta-analyses of the correct effect estimates and standard errors from cRCTs were pooled using generic inverse-variance methods in RevMan 2012. For interventions with multiple comparison groups, all groups that met the inclusion criteria were included in the review and meta-analyses.[31]
elements.reason: The Methods text explicitly describes criteria and processes used to decide which study results could be pooled for each synthesis (e.g. only pooling outcomes measured the same way, handling missing change scores, inclusion of multiple comparison groups), which addresses how studies were deemed eligible for each synthesis.

elements.quote: For trials which had not accounted for clustering, sample size estimates were adjusted for design effect using an 'approximation method'.[27] Effective sample size was calculated for the comparison groups by dividing the original sample size by the design effect. Design effect was calculated as 1 + (M - 1) ICC, where M is the average cluster size and ICC is the intra-cluster correlation coefficient. If primary data was not provided, we attempted to find an appropriate ICC from the literature and adjusted the sample size accordingly.[28] ... Where the change per group was not available [26, 30], we used end-values where randomisation was successful.[26] 95% confidence intervals (CIs) have been reported alongside all effect estimates. Meta-analyses of the correct effect estimates and standard errors from cRCTs were pooled using generic inverse-variance methods in RevMan 2012.
elements.reason: The manuscript describes specific methods to prepare data for synthesis: adjusting sample sizes for clustering (design effect and ICC), substituting end-values when change scores unavailable, reporting 95% CIs, and pooling cRCT estimates using generic inverse-variance — addressing handling of missing summary statistics and data conversions.

elements.quote: In addition, we included a summary of findings table for the primary outcomes of this review (Table 2). It included the number of participants and studies for each outcome, a summary of the intervention effect, and a measure of the quality of evidence for each outcome according to GRADE considerations.
elements.reason: The manuscript explicitly describes tabular structures (summary of findings table/Table 2) and the data included (number of participants and studies, intervention effect, quality of evidence). Table 1 (chunk table_0) further shows a tabular display of study characteristics.

elements.quote: Forest plot was generated for each comparison.
elements.reason: The methods describe graphical methods used to display results (forest plots). Additional figures referenced in the text (PRISMA flow diagram, risk of bias summary figure) are also presented (chunks text_14 and text_15 and associated figures).

elements.quote: Outcomes of interventions identified under the review were grouped into health topics identified in the protocol.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the basis for grouping studies/outcomes (grouped into health topics from the protocol and grouped by type of outcome measured), which indicates how studies were ordered/grouped in tables or syntheses.
No description or justification for using non-standard graphs is provided in the supplied evidence; only standard graphs (forest plots, PRISMA flow, risk-of-bias figure) are mentioned.

elements.quote: Meta-analysis was conducted using Review Manager (Revman) version 5.2.[29]. ... Meta-analyses of the correct effect estimates and standard errors from cRCTs were pooled using generic inverse-variance methods in RevMan 2012.
elements.reason: The report names the software used for meta-analysis (Review Manager/RevMan) and gives specific version references (RevMan version 5.2 and mention of RevMan 2012).

elements.quote: In case of considerable heterogeneity (I 2 > 75%) we only carried out a narrative synthesis of the results and grouped our findings by the type of outcome measured.
elements.reason: When meta-analysis was not appropriate due to high heterogeneity, the authors state they performed a narrative synthesis and grouped findings by outcome, providing a justification linked to I2 > 75%.

elements.quote: We used the random-effects model for all analyses, to incorporate any existing heterogeneity.
elements.reason: The authors report using a random-effects model and explicitly give the rationale (to incorporate existing heterogeneity).

elements.quote: Meta-analyses of the correct effect estimates and standard errors from cRCTs were pooled using generic inverse-variance methods in RevMan 2012. Binary outcomes were reported as relative risk (RR)... For continuous outcomes ... mean difference (MD)... 95% confidence intervals (CIs) have been reported alongside all effect estimates.
elements.reason: The statistical methods for synthesis are described (generic inverse-variance pooling, reporting of RR and MD, and 95% CIs), indicating how effect estimates were calculated and combined.

elements.quote: Heterogeneity among the studies included in meta-analysis was assessed by visual inspection of overlap of confidence intervals, and by assessing statistical heterogeneity with the Chi 2 statistic (P < 0.1). I 2 statistic was computed to quantify heterogeneity; an I 2 of 75% and above was taken as an indicator of more than desired heterogeneity.
elements.reason: The authors report specific methods to identify and quantify heterogeneity: visual inspection, Chi-square test, and I2 statistic with an explicit threshold.
Although the review states a random-effects model was used, no between-study variance estimator (e.g. DerSimonian–Laird, REML, etc.) is named or described in the provided text.
The methods do not specify how confidence intervals for the summary effect were calculated in the random-effects context (no method for CI calculation is reported).

Other implementation details specific to random-effects meta-analysis (e.g. weighting scheme beyond generic inverse-variance, tau-squared estimation settings) are not reported in the provided evidence.
No Bayesian meta-analysis was performed or described in the report, so Bayesian prior specification is not applicable.

elements.quote: For interventions with multiple comparison groups, all groups that met the inclusion criteria were included in the review and meta-analyses.[31] ... comparison groups we combined the relevant experimental and control groups to generate a single pair wise comparison.[31] ... For trials which had not accounted for clustering, sample size estimates were adjusted for design effect using an 'approximation method'. Effective sample size was calculated for the comparison groups by dividing the original sample size by the design effect. Design effect was calculated as 1 + (M - 1) ICC...
elements.reason: The authors describe methods to handle multiple groups and clustering: combining groups into single pairwise comparisons and adjusting sample sizes for cluster trials using design effect/ICC to account for dependency.

elements.quote: Meta-analysis was conducted only for interventions for which there were a minimum of two studies displaying sufficient homogeneity (I 2 statistic < 75%). In case of considerable heterogeneity (I 2 > 75%) we only carried out a narrative synthesis of the results... One trial lacking baseline information collection by investigators was excluded from the meta-analysis.
elements.reason: The authors identify situations where planned meta-analyses were not performed (insufficient homogeneity, single-trial issues, exclusion of a trial lacking baseline data) and provide reasons for these decisions.

elements.quote: In order to compare the different subgroups with each other, we conducted a standard heterogeneity test across the subgroup results, by calculating the I-square statistic. During subgroup analysis, we ensured that the subgroup data being compared were independent. In addition, we also performed a sensitivity analyses to assess the influence of study size and study design on the findings.
elements.reason: The manuscript specifies methods used to explore heterogeneity: I-squared statistic for subgroup heterogeneity, ensuring independence of subgroup data, and sensitivity analyses for study size and design.

elements.quote: Subgroup analyses was performed by the age and sex of participants, and sensitivity analyses was conducted to assess the robustness of the findings.
elements.reason: The factors for subgroup analysis (age and sex) are reported, but no factor levels or any expected direction of effect modification are provided.
No explicit statement reporting whether analyses used study-level variables, within-study contrasts, or both is present in the provided evidence.

elements.quote: In order to compare the different subgroups with each other, we conducted a standard heterogeneity test across the subgroup results, by calculating the I-square statistic.
elements.reason: The manuscript reports the method used to compare subgroup effects: conducting a heterogeneity test across subgroup results using the I-squared statistic.

elements.quote: In case of considerable heterogeneity (I 2 > 75%) we only carried out a narrative synthesis of the results and grouped our findings by the type of outcome measured.
elements.reason: When meta-analysis was unsuitable due to high heterogeneity, the authors describe using a narrative synthesis and grouping findings by outcome type, which is an informal method to explore heterogeneity.
There is no information in the provided evidence identifying which analyses of heterogeneity (if any) were not pre-specified.

elements.quote: 347 Non-Duplicate Citations Screened; 317 Articles Excluded After Title/Abstract Screen
elements.reason: The PRISMA flow diagram (Fig 1) in chunk text_14 explicitly shows the number of non-duplicate records screened (347) and the number excluded after the title/abstract screen (317). elements.quote:
Where the change per group was not available [26, 30], we used end-values where randomisation was successful.[26]
For trials which had not accounted for clustering, sample size estimates were adjusted for design effect using an 'approximation method'.[27] Effective sample size was calculated for the comparison groups by dividing the original sample size by the design effect. Design effect was calculated as 1 + (M - 1) ICC, where M is the average cluster size and ICC is the intra-cluster correlation coefficient. If primary data was not provided, we attempted to find an appropriate ICC from the literature and adjusted the sample size accordingly.[28]

elements.quote: Results of our review are in concordance with that of a Cochrane review by Uthman et al in 2015 which assessed the effects of multiple risk factors intervention for primary prevention of CVDs.[14] Ebrahim in 2011 had also demonstrated similar results.[52] However both these reviews did not focus on the role of CHW as a change agent. Recently two reviews focussing upon this concept have been published [12, 13] but both of these lacked quality of evidence. This adds to the importance of results of the present review.
elements.reason: The discussion explicitly compares the review's findings with prior reviews and other evidence (Cochrane review, Ebrahim 2011, and recent reviews), placing the results in the context of existing literature and noting similarities and differences in focus and quality.

elements.quote: A major limitation observed was the low magnitude of effect and quality of evidence in study trials included in this review. A probable reason could have been the nature of studies (community based studies, as against controlled clinical settings) which dilutes the effect of interventions due to within subject and within cluster differences. Implementation of interventions by less trained staff could also have contributed to a decrease in effect size. Most of the trials reported training the health workers in a workshop or a short course, which could also have affected the performance. With the exception of a trial by Jafar et al, all other included trials relied on short-term effects of interventions and failed to report issues related to behaviour relapse, as in interventions targeting medication adherence, weight loss or smoking. Also, shorter length of follow ups fail to capture 'saturation effects' of primary prevention interventions implemented at population level.[53] ... The differences in study settings, baseline differences, differences in follow up periods or differences in intervention content and delivery methods led to considerable PLOS heterogeneity in evidence. We tried to address this by use of a 'maximum 75% heterogeneity cut-off criteria' for selection of results of risk factors for pooling. The review has also left several questions unanswered, primarily due to paucity of trials, especially in the field of cancer, COPD and stroke. This gap in information needs to be filled, which requires further research using robust trial designs and longer follow-up periods. More good quality trials need to be designed and implemented to study the effects of interventions. Measurement approaches should be made more objective and reliance on self-reported parameters should be reduced in order to enhance methodological robustness of the trials.
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly describes multiple limitations of the included evidence—low effect sizes and low quality, community-based study designs diluting effects, limited training of implementers, short follow-ups, heterogeneity across studies, paucity of trials for some conditions, and measurement/ self-report issues—thereby addressing limitations of the evidence included in the review.

elements.quote: Minor and major methodological challenges in synthesising the evidence should also be understood while interpreting the results of this review. As we combined the results of individual and cluster randomised controlled trials, suitable analytical methods were used to make the trial results comparable. Second, the settings in which the trials were conducted varied despite developing country settings. The type of CHW, nature of interventions also were not exactly similar. The differences in study settings, baseline differences, differences in follow up periods or differences in intervention content and delivery methods led to considerable ... heterogeneity in evidence.
elements.reason: The Discussion explicitly notes limitations of the review's synthesis process (combining individual and cluster RCTs), heterogeneity due to varied settings/interventions, and methodological challenges in synthesising the evidence.

elements.quote: The differences in study settings, baseline differences, differences in follow up periods or differences in intervention content and delivery methods led to considerable ... heterogeneity in evidence. elements.reason: The authors describe consequences of limitations (e.g., resulting heterogeneity) and a mitigation (75% I2 cut-off), but they do not systematically discuss the potential impact of each review-process limitation (for example, impacts of single-reviewer data abstraction or other procedural choices) nor quantify how each limitation might affect certainty of findings; thus the discussion of impacts is partial.

elements.quote: The evidence suggests that the CHWs may be effective in altering the risk factors for NCDs for people in developing countries. While community health workers' led interventions were not very successful in altering individuals' behaviour patterns, modifications in physical parameters, such as systolic and diastolic blood pressure was clearly observed. Community health workers were also able to introduce and sustain a long term control on HbA1C levels among diabetics, however short term effects observed were not statistically significant. It was also observed that while CHW led interventions were able to significantly reduce cholesterol levels among participants, self-efficacy and medication adherence still remain a cause of concern.
elements.reason: Explicit discussion of how CHW interventions affect clinical and behavioral outcomes, describing where they are effective (blood pressure, HbA1C, cholesterol) and where they are less successful (behaviour change, self-efficacy), which informs practical implications for implementation.

elements.quote: As countries turn towards universal healthcare coverage, policymakers will need high quality evidence about efficient strategies for NCDs, particularly those focusing on prevention, to avoid burdening health systems with large numbers of individuals with chronic conditions that are expensive to treat. ... So, in this sense, a process of task shifting will be required in order to extend services to those who need them in the face of a shortage of physicians, nurses, and other higher-level health professionals. This review fulfils a palpable deficiency in terms of evidence of CHW effectiveness from low and middle income countries.
elements.reason: Direct statements addressing policymakers, resource allocation, and task-shifting indicate policy implications and recommendations for health system strategies.

elements.quote: The review has also left several questions unanswered, primarily due to paucity of trials, especially in the field of cancer, COPD and stroke. This gap in information needs to be filled, which requires further research using robust trial designs and longer follow-up periods. More good quality trials need to be designed and implemented to study the effects of interventions. Measurement approaches should be made more objective and reliance on self-reported parameters should be reduced in order to enhance methodological robustness of the trials.
elements.reason: Provides explicit recommendations for future research: need for robust trial designs, longer follow-ups, more trials in certain disease areas, and improved measurement approaches.
